title: The Cochlear Amplifier and Otoacoustic Emissions

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: In a healthy cochlea, high characteristic frequencies lie near the {{c1::base}}, and low ones near the apex.
cards.back: Characteristic frequency is the frequency that produces the greatest motion at a place for soft sounds.
cards.quote: high frequencies near the base, low ones near the apex.

cards.front: Which cochlear hair cells amplify motion, and which send most of the signal to the brain?
cards.back: Outer hair cells amplify; inner hair cells send most of the signal to the brain.
cards.quote: outer hair cells (the three rows that amplify; the single row of inner hair cells sends most of the signal to the brain)

cards.front: A system is {{c1::linear}} when its output keeps a fixed proportion to its input.
cards.quote: A system like that is linear: its output keeps a fixed proportion to its input.
cards.section: A gain that death erases

cards.front: On decibel plots of living and postmortem basilar-membrane motion at the same basal site, how is cochlear amplifier gain read?
cards.back: As the vertical gap: living motion minus postmortem motion in dB at the same sound level.
cards.quote: On decibel axes the gain is the vertical gap between the curves,
cards.section: A gain that death erases

cards.front: Why does cochlear amplification sharpen frequency tuning?
cards.back: Gain is large only near the characteristic frequency, so it raises the travelling-wave peak more than responses away from it.
cards.quote: Because the gain is large only near the characteristic frequency, it sharpens the peak of the travelling wave as well as raising it.
cards.section: A gain that death erases

cards.front: How is shrinking cochlear gain thought to help the ear handle a wide range of sound levels?
cards.back: Motion grows less than sound level over the compressive range, fitting a wide range of sound into a narrower range of motion.
cards.quote: A narrow range of motion is thought to help the hair cells and nerve handle a wide range of loudness.
cards.section: A gain that death erases

cards.front: At a basal site, an extremely soft characteristic-frequency tone lies within the cochlear gain plateau. Its level rises slightly, staying in that plateau. What happens to gain and motion, and why?
cards.back: Gain stays at its maximum and motion grows linearly with input. In the softest range, the gain has stopped increasing.
cards.quote: at the very softest levels it stops rising and levels off at its maximum, and the response is linear again.
cards.section: A gain that death erases

cards.front: At a basal characteristic-frequency site, assume living motion grows 2.5 dB per 10 dB of sound over a 60 dB increase; postmortem motion grows 10 dB per 10 dB. How much does gain change?
cards.back: Living motion rises 60 × (2.5/10) = 15 dB; postmortem motion rises 60 × (10/10) = 60 dB. Gain changes by 15 - 60 = -45 dB: it shrinks by 45 dB.
cards.quote: Suppose the living response grows 2.5 dB for every 10 dB of sound across the middle of the range, a slope of 0.25 (an illustrative value).
cards.section: A gain that death erases

cards.front: Why does a fall in cochlear amplifier gain at louder levels not establish that outer hair cells do less work?
cards.back: Gain is a response ratio, not a work measurement. That ratio can fall without establishing how much work the cells do.
cards.quote: The gain is a ratio, so a falling gain does not by itself mean the cells do less work at high levels.
cards.section: A gain that death erases

cards.front: How would matched living and postmortem basilar-membrane recordings distinguish frequency-selective active gain from broadly enhanced passive motion?
cards.back: Compare soft-tone responses near and well below the same basal site’s characteristic frequency. A large living–dead gap near it but little gap well below supports frequency-selective active gain. The inference combines death-sensitive gain with its frequency selectivity.
cards.quote: Well below the characteristic frequency, the living and dead curves are nearly the same.
cards.section: A gain that death erases

cards.front: An outer hair cell {{c1::shortens}} as it depolarizes and lengthens as it hyperpolarizes.
cards.quote: The cell shortens as it depolarizes and lengthens as it hyperpolarizes,
cards.section: The engine: from a bent bundle to a pushing cell

cards.front: How does bending an outer hair cell bundle toward its tallest stereocilia produce cell-body motion?
cards.back: More transduction channels open; inward current depolarizes the cell. Voltage changes the motor’s shape, shortening the cell so it pushes on the organ of Corti.
cards.quote: Transduction current flows into the cell, so the voltage rises as channels open and falls as they close.
cards.section: The engine: from a bent bundle to a pushing cell

cards.front: An outer hair cell bundle is displaced away from its tallest stereocilia. What happens to its transduction channels, voltage and cell length, and why?
cards.back: Some channels open at rest close, voltage falls and the cell lengthens. Reduced transduction current reverses the voltage-driven shortening pathway.
cards.quote: bending the other way closes some of those open at rest
cards.section: The engine: from a bent bundle to a pushing cell

cards.front: A cochlear amplifier is proposed to add energy on every cycle of a 20 kHz tone. Calculate the time available per cycle and explain the implication for a slow ATP-hydrolysis step.
cards.back: T = 1/f = 1/(20 × 1,000 s⁻¹) = 0.000050 s = 50 microseconds. A slow chemical step cannot be awaited each cycle; this motivates direct voltage drive. It does not resolve high-frequency filtering or motor kinetics.
cards.quote: A tone at 20 kHz, near the top of the human range, completes a cycle every 50 microseconds.
cards.section: The engine: from a bent bundle to a pushing cell

cards.front: Why can a directly voltage-driven outer hair cell motor still receive a smaller electrical drive at high frequencies?
cards.back: Membrane resistance and capacitance smooth fast voltage changes, reducing the voltage swing reaching the motor as frequency rises.
cards.quote: The membrane's resistance and capacitance smooth fast voltage changes, so less of the voltage swing reaches prestin as frequency rises.
cards.section: The engine: from a bent bundle to a pushing cell

cards.front: Membrane capacitance is charge moved per unit voltage change: {{c1::C = dQ/dV}}.
cards.quote: Through capacitance, the charge moved per unit change of voltage, C = dQ/dV.
cards.section: Reading the motor's fingerprint: nonlinear capacitance

cards.front: What does the nonlinear-capacitance bell of a prestin-expressing cell report?
cards.back: Voltage-dependent displacement of charge within prestin; its peak marks the voltage where charge changes most readily.
cards.quote: The usual reading is that it reports voltage-dependent displacement of charge in the protein.
cards.section: Reading the motor's fingerprint: nonlinear capacitance

cards.front: Why does an S-shaped prestin charge–voltage curve produce bell-shaped nonlinear capacitance?
cards.back: Capacitance is the slope of charge versus voltage. That slope is greatest at the S-curve midpoint and falls on either side.
cards.quote: The slope of that S is largest at its midpoint and falls on both sides, so the extra capacitance is a bell.
cards.section: Reading the motor's fingerprint: nonlinear capacitance

cards.front: In the two-state prestin model, what are contracted-state occupancy and normalized nonlinear capacitance at the half-activation voltage Vh?
cards.back: Occupancy f = 0.5; normalized nonlinear capacitance = 1, its peak.
cards.quote: The exponent is zero, so f = 0.5 and normalized NLC = 4 x 0.5 x 0.5 = 1, the peak.
cards.section: Reading the motor's fingerprint: nonlinear capacitance

cards.front: For gerbil prestin in the stated cell-line model at 295 K, use Vh = -112 mV, z = 0.70 and kT/e = 25.42 mV. At V = -62 mV, find f = 1/[1 + exp(-z(V - Vh)/(kT/e))] and normalized NLC = 4f(1 - f). Assume equilibrium, no linear capacitance and no kinetics.
cards.back: V - Vh = +50 mV; exponent = -0.70 × 50/25.42 ≈ -1.377. Thus f ≈ 0.798, and 4f(1 - f) ≈ 0.644, about 64% of peak. These are cell-line model values, not an in vivo operating point.
cards.quote: Assume 295 K, a two-state equilibrium, no linear capacitance and no kinetics, so kT/e = 25.42 mV.
cards.section: Reading the motor's fingerprint: nonlinear capacitance

cards.front: In a two-state prestin model with fixed thermal voltage and Vh, effective valence z increases from 0.70 to 1.40. What happens to nonlinear-capacitance width, and why?
cards.back: The width halves. The model’s half-height width scales as 1/z: increasing effective charge steepens the occupancy curve and concentrates charge movement into a narrower voltage range.
cards.quote: A larger z makes the S steeper, so the charge moves over a smaller range of voltage.
cards.section: Reading the motor's fingerprint: nonlinear capacitance

cards.front: A prestin variant retains a normal equilibrium nonlinear-capacitance curve in cultured cells. Is that enough to conclude it can supply normal cycle-by-cycle cochlear power at high frequencies?
cards.back: No. NLC reports charge movement, not force or power; equilibrium fits omit kinetics, and membrane filtering reduces high-frequency drive. Combining these rules requires mechanical and frequency-dependent measurements before concluding power is normal.
cards.quote: Nor do they say how much force or power a hair cell produces.
cards.section: Reading the motor's fingerprint: nonlinear capacitance

cards.front: What composite voltage sensor did the dolphin prestin structural study propose?
cards.back: A bound anion, the charged residues that hold it, and a helix dipole.
cards.quote: The dolphin study proposed a composite sensor: a bound anion, the charged residues that hold it, and a helix dipole.
cards.section: What the structures can and cannot show

cards.front: How could the membrane-area change suggested by human prestin structures change outer hair cell length?
cards.back: If many side-wall prestin molecules change their membrane footprint together, the wall’s area changes and the cell’s length changes with it.
cards.quote: when many prestin molecules in the side wall change their area together, the wall's area changes, and the cell's length with it.
cards.section: What the structures can and cannot show

cards.front: Human prestin structures stabilized with chloride and salicylate differ in membrane footprint. What additional observations would test whether these candidate states describe a voltage-driven motor stroke in an outer hair cell?
cards.back: Measure voltage-driven changes in prestin’s membrane footprint together with cell shortening and mechanical work in a hair cell. The design combines the area-motor proposal with the rule that ligand-stabilized endpoints alone establish neither a physiological stroke nor work.
cards.quote: Each structure is a candidate end state, not a recording of a working motor.
cards.section: What the structures can and cannot show

cards.front: What mainly generates click-evoked versus distortion-product otoacoustic emissions?
cards.back: Click-evoked emissions mainly arise from travelling-wave reflection near its peak; distortion products mainly arise from cochlear nonlinearity. Both depend on the active process.
cards.quote: Distortion-product emissions arise mainly from the cochlea's nonlinearity. Both depend on the active process.
cards.section: The sound that comes back

cards.front: Two pure tones enter a cochlea, and their summed waveform reaches the curved part of its fast saturating response. What happens to the output frequencies compared with a linear response, and why?
cards.back: New frequencies appear because instantaneous waveform distortion mixes the tones. A linear response would return only the input frequencies.
cards.quote: the squashed waveform contains frequencies the stimulus did not. A linear system gives back only f1 and f2.
cards.section: The sound that comes back

cards.front: For an invented ear-canal test with f1 = 2,000 Hz and f2 = 2,400 Hz, calculate the cubic distortion product 2f1 - f2. Was that frequency present in the stimulus?
cards.back: 2f1 - f2 = 2 × 2,000 - 2,400 = 1,600 Hz. Neither input tone was at 1,600 Hz; the nonlinearity creates this product.
cards.quote: 2 x 2,000 - 2,400 = 1,600 Hz, a frequency the stimulus did not contain.
cards.section: The sound that comes back

cards.front: A cochlea produces a distortion-product emission at moderate stimulus levels. After death, the same tones are repeated. What happens to the product, and why?
cards.back: It is usually greatly reduced or undetectable. Death removes the living electrical drive and mechanical amplification that support the emission at these levels.
cards.quote: at these moderate levels the distortion product in the ear canal is greatly reduced or undetectable after death.
cards.section: The sound that comes back

cards.front: An ear produces a normal screening emission, but a scalp recording shows very abnormal synchronous auditory nerve and brainstem activity. Which stage remains functional, and why can hearing still be impaired?
cards.back: Outer hair cell activity can produce sound through the middle ear, while neural transmission may be abnormal. Combining emission generation with the brainstem response’s neural requirement explains why a screening pass cannot establish intact hearing.
cards.quote: A screening pass shows that outer hair cell activity can produce an emission through the middle ear.
cards.section: The sound that comes back

cards.front: A mouse lacking prestin still produces distortion-product emissions at high stimulus levels. What does this show about the product’s dependence on the motor?
cards.back: At high levels, a distortion-generating nonlinearity can remain without prestin. The result does not establish normal amplification or normal low-to-moderate-level screening emissions.
cards.quote: in mice lacking prestin, distortion-product emissions still appear at high levels
cards.section: The sound that comes back

cards.front: Why does compressive growth of cochlear motion alone not prove that individual waveforms are distorted?
cards.back: A slow volume control can compress the input–output relation without acting fast enough to reshape each waveform and create new frequencies.
cards.quote: a slow volume control could compress motion without making new tones
cards.section: The sound that comes back

cards.front: A hair bundle is driven by a flexible probe. Over steady cycles it loses more energy to fluid drag than the probe supplies. What does the energy balance show?
cards.back: The bundle adds energy and is active. A passive bundle cannot dissipate more than its supplied energy over steady cycles; large displacement alone would not establish this.
cards.quote: Over steady cycles, a passive bundle cannot lose more energy to drag than the probe puts in.
cards.section: A second engine? The frog hair bundle

cards.front: Why does loss of cochlear amplification in a prestin knock-in mouse with normal transduction and cell mechanics support a requirement for somatic motility?
cards.back: Preserving transduction and cell mechanics while losing amplification isolates the missing voltage-driven cell-body motility as necessary for mammalian cochlear amplification.
cards.quote: transduction and cell mechanics were normal, yet amplification was lost much as in a knockout, so somatic motility is necessary
cards.section: A second engine? The frog hair bundle

cards.front: A simple noise-free hair-bundle model sits exactly at a Hopf bifurcation and is driven at its natural frequency. Its motion grows as the cube root of drive. For 30 dB more drive, how many dB more motion does the model predict?
cards.back: The cube-root rule gives a dB slope of 1/3, so motion rises by 30/3 = 10 dB. This is a model prediction under the stated conditions, not a measured mammalian slope.
cards.quote: the response grows as the cube root of its drive, so 30 dB more drive gives only 10 dB more motion.
cards.section: A second engine? The frog hair bundle

cards.front: Suppose a selective perturbation prevents hair-cell transduction-channel gating. Could a loss of cochlear gain alone distinguish a bundle engine from the prestin cell-body engine, and why?
cards.back: No; both candidate engines can be disrupted. The stated rules are that transduction current supplies prestin’s voltage drive, while channel gating and adaptation can move the bundle. A shared upstream perturbation cannot isolate their contributions.
cards.quote: Both engines depend on the transduction channel. Its current sets the voltage that drives prestin, and its gating and adaptation can move the bundle.
cards.section: A second engine? The frog hair bundle

cards.front: The top surface of the organ of Corti, where the hair bundles sit, is the {{c1::reticular lamina}}.
cards.quote: The reticular lamina is the top surface of the organ of Corti, where the hair bundles sit.
cards.section: Where along the cochlea is the gain gathered?

cards.front: The cochlear {{c1::buildup distance}} is the length basal to the travelling-wave peak over which gain is gathered.
cards.quote: The buildup distance is the length of cochlea, basal to the peak, over which the gain is gathered.
cards.section: Where along the cochlea is the gain gathered?

cards.front: Near-basal suppressors reduce a probe response, whereas distant-basal suppressors do not. What controls are needed before interpreting this as gain building over a limited stretch of cochlea?
cards.back: Check that suppressors reduce outer hair cell force where targeted and barely move the probe site themselves; vary levels and measure suppressor excitation. Combine those controls with distance-dependent suppression to support limited buildup. Add matched postmortem recordings to test dependence on living activity.
cards.quote: suppression confined to nearby suppressors supports a limited buildup only if the distant ones were effective in the regions tested.
cards.section: Where along the cochlea is the gain gathered?

cards.front: At a matched cochlear site, reticular-lamina motion exceeds basilar-membrane motion in life, and the difference disappears after death. What does this establish, and does it locate the energy source?
cards.back: The differential motion depends on the living state, and the organ of Corti is not moving as one block. It does not locate the energy source or divide work between bundles and cell bodies; motion is not work.
cards.quote: a difference that vanishes after death depends on the living state, and larger reticular-lamina motion shows the organ of Corti is not moving as one block.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: A gerbil prestin anion-site mutant retains nonlinear capacitance in salicylate. Before using this drug insensitivity to argue against a chloride-only voltage sensor, what controls are required?
cards.back: Verify expression, localization and baseline nonlinear capacitance for each mutant. Without these controls, the drug response cannot be interpreted as a specific sensor result.
cards.quote: you need expression, localization and baseline NLC for each mutant.
cards.section: The prestin structures, study by study

cards.front: How does medial olivocochlear acetylcholine release reduce outer hair cell amplifier gain?
cards.back: Nicotinic receptors admit calcium, activating nearby calcium-dependent potassium channels. Shunting and hyperpolarization shrink the voltage swing driving prestin, reducing electromotility and gain.
cards.quote: Calcium entry activates nearby calcium-dependent potassium channels.
cards.section: Efferent feedback: turning the gain down

cards.front: A feedback signal increases potassium-channel activity in an outer hair cell, shunting and hyperpolarizing it. What happens to voltage-driven motion and amplifier gain, and why?
cards.back: Both decrease because the shunt and hyperpolarization shrink the voltage swing that drives the cell’s motor.
cards.quote: By shunting and hyperpolarizing the cell, acetylcholine shrinks the voltage swing that drives prestin,
cards.section: Efferent feedback: turning the gain down

cards.front: In the Boero et al. (2018) mouse noise-exposure study, wild-type hearing thresholds recovered but ribbon synapses were lost. Why is threshold recovery insufficient to claim complete recovery?
cards.back: Recovered thresholds coexisted with synapse loss. The result shows that threshold recovery need not mean all noise-related damage has reversed in that mouse protocol.
cards.quote: Wild-type mice recovered thresholds but lost ribbon synapses.
cards.section: Efferent feedback: turning the gain down
